title: Amritsar, 1978
hookLine: a clash between Sikhs and the Sant Nirankari sect left people dead and tensions rising

cards: Vaisakhi, the spring festival, the day Sikhs remember the birth of the Khalsa. Amritsar is full of pilgrims.

And across the city, a different group is holding its own gathering: the Sant Nirankaris, followers of a living guru. To some Sikhs, holding that gathering in the Guru's own city, on that day, is an insult.
A group of Sikhs sets out to protest. By evening, people are dead, and the city is not the same.

teach.h: A LIVING GURU, AND THE GURU GRANTH.
teach.b: First, the quarrel. Sikhs hold that the line of human Gurus ended with Guru Gobind Singh, and that the Guru now lives in the Guru Granth Sahib and in the Khalsa panth.

The Sant Nirankaris followed a living guru of their own, and some Sikhs heard things said in their gatherings as mocking the Sikh Gurus. The Nirankaris saw themselves as a spiritual movement free to teach as they chose.
Sikhs from the Akhand Kirtani Jatha, and followers of Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, head of the Damdami Taksal, marched toward the Nirankari gathering to protest. Shots were fired.
Sikh protesters were killed, and so were some Nirankaris. Accounts still differ about who struck first. Third, what followed: courts, edicts and anger.
The Akal Takht issued a hukamnama telling Sikhs to keep away from the Nirankaris. Bhindranwale's voice grew louder, and violence between the two groups went on. Fourth, the root.
Among Sheikh Farid's verses in the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 1382, is a short one: do good even to the one who does you wrong, and don't let anger settle in your mind.

That line had stood in the Guru Granth Sahib for centuries before that Vaisakhi. The story of these years is partly the story of how hard that line is to live when people feel their Guru has been insulted.
Remembering the day honestly means holding the grief of every family who lost someone in it.

how: Some histories of Punjab treat the Vaisakhi clash in Amritsar as a turning point toward the conflict that followed; those killed among the protesters are remembered in some Sikh circles as martyrs.

games.q: it's Vaisakhi in Amritsar. some Sikhs believe a gathering across the city mocks the Gurus. what happened next?
o: the gathering was left alone, and the festival went on.
a group of Sikhs marched to protest, and shots were fired.
the two groups met and made peace.
games.why: a group of Sikhs marched to protest. shots were fired, people died on both sides, and tension rose across Punjab.

practice: Bring to mind two groups who don't trust each other, in your town, your family, your country, anywhere, and don't decide who's right.

Breathe in and see one ordinary person from the first group at their own kitchen table; breathe out and see one from the second at theirs, then hold both tables at once and wish them both a quiet evening.
If you pray, pray for peace between them in your own words, or rest on Waheguru.
